'''''Metamagical Themas''''' is an eclectic collection of articles that [[Douglas Hofstadter]] wrote for the [[popular science]] magazine ''[[Scientific American]]'' during the early 1980s. The anthology was published in 1985 by [[Basic Books]].

The volume is substantial in size and contains extensive notes concerning responses to the articles and other information relevant to their content.  (One of the notes—page 65—suggested [[memetics]] for the study of [[memes]].)

==Contents==
Major themes of the columns include self-reference in [[meme]]s, language, art and logic; discussions of philosophical issues important in cognitive science/AI; analogies and what makes something similar to something else (specifically what makes, for example, an uppercase letter 'A' recognizable as such) <ref>[[#Metamagical|Metamagical Themas]], ch 13.</ref>; and lengthy discussions of the work of [[Robert Axelrod (political scientist)|Robert Axelrod]] on the [[prisoner's dilemma]], as well as the idea of [[superrationality]].<ref>[[#Metamagical|Metamagical Themas]], ch. 29</ref>

The concept of superrationality, and its relevance to the [[Cold War]], environmental issues and such, is accompanied by notes on experiments conducted by the author at the time<ref>[[#Metamagical|Metamagical Themas]], ch 32.</ref>. Another notable feature is the inclusion of two dialogues in the style of those appearing in ''[[Gödel, Escher, Bach]]''. [[Ambigram]]s are mentioned.

There are three articles centered on the [[Lisp programming language]], in which Hofstadter first details the language itself, and then shows how it relates to [[Gödel's incompleteness theorem]]. Two articles are devoted to [[Rubik's Cube]] and similar puzzles. Many chapters open with an illustration of an extremely abstract alphabet, yet one which is still [[Gestalt psychology|gestaltly]] recognizable as such.

The game of [[Nomic]] was first introduced to the public in this column, in June 1982, when excerpts from a book (still unpublished at the time) by the game's creator [[Peter Suber]] were printed and discussed.

The index of the book mentions Hofstadter's recurring alter ego, [[Egbert B. Gebstadter]], whose "book" is also referenced in the Bibliography.

==List of Hofstadter's "Metamagical Themas" Chapters==
From January 1957 through December 1980, [[Martin Gardner]]'s "[[List of Martin Gardner Mathematical Games columns|Mathematical Games]]" column was a monthly feature in ''[[Scientific American]]'' magazine. In 1981, Gardner's column alternated with a new column by Hofstadter called "Metamagical Themas" (an [[anagram]] of "Mathematical Games"). Then Hofstadter's column appeared monthly from January 1982 through July 1983.<ref>[http://www.scientificamerican.com/author/douglas-r-hofstadter/ "Stories by Douglas R. Hofstadter"]. ''Scientific American''.</ref>

The Chapters were re-ordered so that they could be grouped more cohesively into seven Sections. A ''Post Scriptum'' was added to each chapter often detailing correspondence with readers after the publication of the column.

==French edition==
''Metamagical Themas'' was also published in French, under the title ''Ma Thémagie'' (InterEditions, 1988), the translators being Jean-Baptiste Berthelin, Jean-Luc Bonnetain, and Lise Rosenbaum.

Hofstadter talks of the challenges of translating this book in his subsequent work on translation, Le Ton Beau de Marot. <ref>{{cite book |last=Hofstadter |first=Douglas R. |title=Le Ton beau de Marot: In Praise of the Music of Language |publisher=Basic Books |year=1997 |isbn=978-0-465-08645-0}}</ref>

==Reception==
[[David Langford|Dave Langford]] reviewed ''Metamagical Themas'' for ''[[White Dwarf (magazine)|White Dwarf]]'' #88, and stated that "a heady mixture of computers, art, mathematics, philosophy, jokes and above all games."<ref name="WD88">{{cite magazine  | last =Langford | first =Dave | author-link =David Langford | title =Critical Mass  | magazine =[[White Dwarf (magazine)|White Dwarf]]  | issue =88  | pages =8   | publisher =[[Games Workshop]]  | date = April 1987  }}</ref>

[[Martin Gardner]], the creator of the Mathematical column in Scientific American said “The incredible Dr. Hofstadter is back, in golden-braid form, with a collection of wide-ranging essays that swarm with extraordinary ideas, brilliant fables, deep philosophical questions and Carrollian word play.” <ref>{{Cite web |date=April 1985 |title=Metamagical Themas, Questing for the Essence of Mind and Pattern |url=https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/douglas-r-hofstadter/metamagical-themas/9780786723867/?lens=basic-books |website=Hachette Books}}</ref>
